title: Interpret basic operations of Rapid PVST+ Spanning Tree Protocol

questions.question: What problem does STP solve?
questions.explanation: STP prevents Layer 2 loops by blocking redundant paths.

correct.explanation: STP blocks redundant Layer 2 paths so frames cannot loop endlessly through a switched topology.

incorrect.explanation: Routing loops are a Layer 3 problem (TTL, routing protocol convergence) — STP operates at Layer 2 on switches.
incorrect.misconceptionTested: Applying STP to Layer 3 routing loops
incorrect.whatItDoes: Routing loops points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for stp purpose.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "stp purpose", Layer 2 switching loops satisfies what this question tests — Routing loops does not.

incorrect.explanation: IP conflicts are addressed by DHCP snooping, DAI, or manual assignment — STP does not detect duplicate IPs.
incorrect.misconceptionTested: Expecting STP to fix IP addressing conflicts
incorrect.whatItDoes: IP address conflicts shifts the answer to IP/Layer 3 addressing instead of Ethernet MAC learning.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: This is a Layer 2 process (stp purpose). Layer 2 switching loops uses Ethernet addresses — not IP headers.

incorrect.explanation: DNS resolution speed is unrelated — STP prevents broadcast/multicast storms from physical switching loops.
incorrect.misconceptionTested: Dragging unrelated services into STP purpose
incorrect.whatItDoes: Slow DNS points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for stp purpose.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "stp purpose", Layer 2 switching loops satisfies what this question tests — Slow DNS does not.

answerReview.examTip: STP: blocking prevents L2 loops — not “drop all user traffic” on a forwarding port.

questions.question: How is the root bridge chosen?
questions.explanation: The lowest Bridge ID (priority, then MAC) wins the root election.

correct.explanation: STP elects the root bridge with the lowest Bridge ID — priority (default 32768) plus switch MAC address.

incorrect.explanation: Highest priority does not win — STP prefers the lowest Bridge ID (priority + MAC).
incorrect.whatItDoes: Highest priority points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for root election.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "root election", Lowest Bridge ID (priority + MAC) satisfies what this question tests — Highest priority does not.

incorrect.explanation: MAC alone is not the sole criterion — Bridge ID combines configurable priority with the system MAC.
incorrect.misconceptionTested: Selecting highest MAC as root tie-break only
incorrect.whatItDoes: Highest MAC points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for root election.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "root election", Lowest Bridge ID (priority + MAC) satisfies what this question tests — Highest MAC does not.

incorrect.explanation: CPU speed is irrelevant to STP root election — Bridge ID determines the root.
incorrect.misconceptionTested: Expecting fastest switch to become root
incorrect.whatItDoes: Fastest CPU points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for root election.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "root election", Lowest Bridge ID (priority + MAC) satisfies what this question tests — Fastest CPU does not.

answerReview.examTip: Root bridge = lowest Bridge ID (priority + MAC).

questions.question: What is the default STP bridge priority?
questions.explanation: Default priority is 32768 (lower is preferred).

correct.explanation: Default STP bridge priority is 32768 — lower numeric value wins root election (often set in increments of 4096).

incorrect.explanation: Priority 0 is the minimum (best) but not the default — Cisco ships switches at 32768 unless changed.
incorrect.misconceptionTested: Confusing best possible priority with factory default
incorrect.whatItDoes: 0 gives a numeric value (timer, prefix, or rate) that may not match the fact tested in default priority.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "default priority", 32768 satisfies what this question tests — 0 does not.

incorrect.explanation: 4096 is a common increment when lowering priority — the default starting value is 32768.
incorrect.misconceptionTested: Using common increment step as default priority
incorrect.whatItDoes: 4096 gives a numeric value (timer, prefix, or rate) that may not match the fact tested in default priority.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "default priority", 32768 satisfies what this question tests — 4096 does not.

incorrect.explanation: 65535 exceeds the valid STP priority range (0–61440 in multiples of 4096) — default is 32768.
incorrect.misconceptionTested: Picking max 16-bit value instead of Cisco default
incorrect.whatItDoes: 65535 gives a numeric value (timer, prefix, or rate) that may not match the fact tested in default priority.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "default priority", 32768 satisfies what this question tests — 65535 does not.

answerReview.examTip: Default STP priority = 32768. Lower wins. Adjust in steps of 4096.

questions.question: Each non-root switch has exactly one of which port type toward the root?
questions.explanation: Each non-root switch has one root port — its lowest-cost path to root.

correct.explanation: Each non-root switch selects exactly one root port — the best path toward the root bridge.

incorrect.explanation: Designated ports face away from the root on each segment — only one root port per non-root switch points toward the root.
incorrect.misconceptionTested: Confusing designated port with root port role
incorrect.whatItDoes: Designated port points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for port roles.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "port roles", Root port satisfies what this question tests — Designated port does not.

incorrect.explanation: Blocking is a port state, not the single best-path port role toward the root — that role is root port.
incorrect.misconceptionTested: Naming blocking as the toward-root port type
incorrect.whatItDoes: Blocking port points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for port roles.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "port roles", Root port satisfies what this question tests — Blocking port does not.

incorrect.explanation: Trunk is an interface mode — STP port roles are root, designated, alternate, or backup.
incorrect.misconceptionTested: Equating trunk mode with STP root port
incorrect.whatItDoes: Trunk port expects VLAN tags on a link that should behave as access-only in this stem.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "port roles", Root port satisfies what this question tests — Trunk port does not.

answerReview.examTip: Non-root switch → one root port (best path to root).

questions.question: PortFast should be enabled on which ports?
questions.explanation: PortFast belongs on access ports to hosts; on switch links it risks loops.

correct.explanation: PortFast skips listening/learning on access ports connected to end hosts — never on switch-to-switch trunks.

incorrect.explanation: Trunks interconnect switches — PortFast on uplinks risks temporary loops if BPDUs are missed; keep PortFast on edge access ports only.
incorrect.whatItDoes: Switch-to-switch trunks expects VLAN tags on a link that should behave as access-only in this stem.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: This stem (portfast) targets access-port behavior — Access ports to end devices is correct; Switch-to-switch trunks applies trunk tagging where a single VLAN is expected.

incorrect.explanation: Router uplinks are not the classic PortFast use case — Cisco guidance targets access ports to PCs, phones, and servers.
incorrect.whatItDoes: Router uplinks points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for portfast.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "portfast", Access ports to end devices satisfies what this question tests — Router uplinks does not.

incorrect.explanation: PortFast on every port including trunks is unsafe — STP needs normal transitions on inter-switch links.
incorrect.whatItDoes: All ports describes flooding the frame to multiple ports in the VLAN.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "portfast", Access ports to end devices satisfies what this question tests — All ports does not.

answerReview.examTip: PortFast → access ports to end devices; pair with BPDU Guard on edges.

questions.question: A PortFast access port receives a BPDU with BPDU Guard enabled. What happens?
questions.explanation: BPDU Guard err-disables the port, protecting against a rogue switch.

correct.explanation: BPDU Guard on a PortFast port err-disables the interface when any BPDU arrives — protects against rogue switches on access ports.

incorrect.explanation: Receiving a BPDU does not make the port root — BPDU Guard shuts the port down immediately.
incorrect.misconceptionTested: Expecting BPDU to trigger root election on access port
incorrect.whatItDoes: Port becomes root points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for bpdu guard.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "bpdu guard", Port is err-disabled (shut down) satisfies what this question tests — Port becomes root does not.

incorrect.explanation: BPDU Guard blocks BPDUs by err-disabling the port — it does not forward them into the STP domain.
incorrect.misconceptionTested: Believing BPDU Guard forwards BPDUs normally
incorrect.whatItDoes: BPDU is forwarded points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for bpdu guard.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "bpdu guard", Port is err-disabled (shut down) satisfies what this question tests — BPDU is forwarded does not.

incorrect.explanation: A BPDU on a PortFast+BPDU Guard port triggers immediate err-disable — this is not a no-op.
incorrect.misconceptionTested: Thinking PortFast ignores all BPDU handling
incorrect.whatItDoes: Nothing points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for bpdu guard.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "bpdu guard", Port is err-disabled (shut down) satisfies what this question tests — Nothing does not.

answerReview.examTip: PortFast + BPDU Guard + BPDU received → err-disable the port.

questions.question: What is the Cisco default spanning-tree mode?
questions.explanation: Rapid PVST+ is the Cisco default — per-VLAN rapid spanning tree.

correct.explanation: Modern Cisco switches default to Rapid PVST+ — per-VLAN rapid spanning tree (802.1w behavior).

incorrect.explanation: 802.1D is classic STP — Cisco defaults to Rapid PVST+, not legacy 802.1D-only mode.
incorrect.whatItDoes: 802.1D points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for rapid pvst.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "rapid pvst", Rapid PVST+ satisfies what this question tests — 802.1D does not.

incorrect.explanation: MST (802.1s) maps multiple VLANs to instances — it is not the factory default on most Catalyst platforms.
incorrect.misconceptionTested: Believing MST is the Cisco default
incorrect.whatItDoes: MST points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for rapid pvst.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "rapid pvst", Rapid PVST+ satisfies what this question tests — MST does not.

incorrect.explanation: PVST (non-rapid) is older per-VLAN STP — current IOS defaults to Rapid PVST+.
incorrect.whatItDoes: PVST points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for rapid pvst.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "rapid pvst", Rapid PVST+ satisfies what this question tests — PVST does not.

answerReview.examTip: Cisco default STP mode → Rapid PVST+.

questions.question: Which command makes a switch the root for VLAN 1 by lowering its priority?
questions.explanation: spanning-tree vlan 1 root primary lowers the priority so this switch becomes root.

correct.explanation: spanning-tree vlan 1 root primary lowers bridge priority to make this switch the root for VLAN 1.

incorrect.explanation: spanning-tree portfast speeds access port transition — doesn't affect root election.
incorrect.whatItDoes: spanning-tree portfast points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for set root.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "set root", spanning-tree vlan 1 root primary satisfies what this question tests — spanning-tree portfast does not.

incorrect.explanation: spanning-tree bpduguard enable protects access ports — not root bridge selection.
incorrect.whatItDoes: spanning-tree bpduguard enable points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for set root.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "set root", spanning-tree vlan 1 root primary satisfies what this question tests — spanning-tree bpduguard enable does not.

incorrect.explanation: switchport mode trunk configures trunking — not STP root priority.
incorrect.whatItDoes: switchport mode trunk expects VLAN tags on a link that should behave as access-only in this stem.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "set root", spanning-tree vlan 1 root primary satisfies what this question tests — switchport mode trunk does not.

answerReview.examTip: Root bridge: lowest bridge priority wins — spanning-tree vlan X root primary sets 24576.

questions.question: What is the IEEE specification for Spanning Tree Protocol (STP)?
questions.explanation: The correct answer follows the source explanation for this objective-aligned question.

correct.explanation: Classic STP is IEEE 802.1D — the original spanning-tree standard (convergence ~30–50 s).

incorrect.explanation: 802.1X is port-based network access control (authentication) — not spanning tree.
incorrect.whatItDoes: 802.1X points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for specification.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "specification", 802.1D satisfies what this question tests — 802.1X does not.

incorrect.explanation: 802.1w is RSTP (rapid STP) — 802.1D is classic STP.
incorrect.whatItDoes: 802.1w points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for specification.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "specification", 802.1D satisfies what this question tests — 802.1w does not.

incorrect.explanation: 802.1s is MST (Multiple Spanning Tree) — classic STP = 802.1D.
incorrect.whatItDoes: 802.1s points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for specification.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "specification", 802.1D satisfies what this question tests — 802.1s does not.

answerReview.examTip: STP standards map: 802.1D = STP | 802.1w = RSTP | 802.1s = MST.

questions.question: Which statement is correct about STP?
choices: STP runs on a central switch by creating a topology database.
STP runs as a distributed process on each switch and creates a topology database.
STP uses routing protocols to check for network loops.
STP uses the MAC address table to check for switching loops.
questions.explanation: The correct answer follows the source explanation for this objective-aligned question.

correct.explanation: STP is distributed — every switch runs the algorithm locally and builds its own STP topology view from BPDUs.

incorrect.explanation: No central STP controller — each switch independently processes BPDUs and elects root/roles.
incorrect.misconceptionTested: Central switch runs STP for all
incorrect.whatItDoes: STP runs on a central switch by creating a topology database. points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for statement.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "statement", STP runs as a distributed process on each switch and creates a topology database. satisfies what this question tests — STP runs on a central switch by creating a topology database. does not.

incorrect.explanation: STP is Layer 2 — it does not use routing protocols to detect switching loops.
incorrect.misconceptionTested: Routing protocols for STP loop detection
incorrect.whatItDoes: STP uses routing protocols to check for network loops. points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for statement.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "statement", STP runs as a distributed process on each switch and creates a topology database. satisfies what this question tests — STP uses routing protocols to check for network loops. does not.

incorrect.explanation: The MAC table forwards frames — STP logic uses BPDUs, not MAC learning, to block loops.
incorrect.misconceptionTested: MAC table as STP loop detector
incorrect.whatItDoes: STP uses the MAC address table to check for switching loops. expects router forwarding to use a MAC/CAM table lookup.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "statement", STP runs as a distributed process on each switch and creates a topology database. satisfies what this question tests — STP uses the MAC address table to check for switching loops. does not.

answerReview.examTip: STP = per-switch BPDU processing → elect root → assign port roles/states.

questions.question: How does STP detect and monitor loops in networks?
choices: STP detects and monitors BPDUs being received on multiple interfaces.
STP detects and monitors normal traffic frames being received on multiple interfaces.
STP detects and monitors CDP frames being received on multiple interfaces.
STP detects and monitors access ports in the same VLAN.
questions.explanation: The correct answer follows the source explanation for this objective-aligned question.

correct.explanation: STP watches BPDUs on ports — duplicate root/path info on multiple interfaces signals a potential L2 loop.

incorrect.explanation: STP does not monitor user data frames for loops — control plane uses BPDUs only.
incorrect.whatItDoes: STP detects and monitors normal traffic frames being received on multiple interfaces. points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for networks.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "networks", STP detects and monitors BPDUs being received on multiple interfaces. satisfies what this question tests — STP detects and monitors normal traffic frames being received on multiple interfaces. does not.

incorrect.explanation: CDP is neighbor discovery — STP loop detection relies on BPDUs, not CDP.
incorrect.misconceptionTested: CDP frames for STP loop detection
incorrect.whatItDoes: STP detects and monitors CDP frames being received on multiple interfaces. points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for networks.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "networks", STP detects and monitors BPDUs being received on multiple interfaces. satisfies what this question tests — STP detects and monitors CDP frames being received on multiple interfaces. does not.

incorrect.explanation: Access ports in the same VLAN do not define STP loop detection — BPDU exchange between bridges does.
incorrect.misconceptionTested: Access port VLAN membership as STP monitor
incorrect.whatItDoes: STP detects and monitors access ports in the same VLAN. treats the port as a single-VLAN access link without 802.1Q tagging.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "networks", STP detects and monitors BPDUs being received on multiple interfaces. satisfies what this question tests — STP detects and monitors access ports in the same VLAN. does not.

answerReview.examTip: STP control plane = BPDUs. Data frames are forwarded separately by the MAC table.

questions.question: What is the link cost with respect to STP?
choices: Link cost is the latency of a frame traversing across the link.

Link cost is the monetary cost to traverse a link.

incorrect.explanation: STP cost is not latency — it is derived from port speed (bandwidth-based cost).
incorrect.whatItDoes: Link cost is the latency of a frame traversing across the link. points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for explanation.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "explanation", Link cost is a numeric value associated with the speed of a link. satisfies what this question tests — Link cost is the latency of a frame traversing across the link. does not.

incorrect.explanation: Summing ports to root is path cost, not the per-link cost definition.
incorrect.misconceptionTested: Path cost definition as link cost
incorrect.whatItDoes: Link cost is the calculation of all the ports in the path to the root bridge. implies many-inside-to-few-outside PAT/overload translation.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "explanation", Link cost is a numeric value associated with the speed of a link. satisfies what this question tests — Link cost is the calculation of all the ports in the path to the root bridge. does not.

incorrect.explanation: STP cost is a technical metric, not a monetary value.
incorrect.misconceptionTested: Monetary cost for STP link cost
incorrect.whatItDoes: Link cost is the monetary cost to traverse a link. points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for explanation.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "explanation", Link cost is a numeric value associated with the speed of a link. satisfies what this question tests — Link cost is the monetary cost to traverse a link. does not.

answerReview.examTip: Per-port link cost (speed) → summed into path cost to root bridge.

questions.question: What is the path cost with respect to RSTP?

incorrect.explanation: Path cost is not latency — it is accumulated STP port costs to the root.
incorrect.whatItDoes: Path cost is the latency of a frame traversing across the link. implies many-inside-to-few-outside PAT/overload translation.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "explanation", Path cost is the calculation of all the ports in the path to the root bridge. satisfies what this question tests — Path cost is the latency of a frame traversing across the link. does not.

incorrect.explanation: STP metrics are not monetary — path cost is the numeric sum of link costs.
incorrect.whatItDoes: Path cost is the monetary cost to traverse a link. implies many-inside-to-few-outside PAT/overload translation.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "explanation", Path cost is the calculation of all the ports in the path to the root bridge. satisfies what this question tests — Path cost is the monetary cost to traverse a link. does not.

incorrect.explanation: A single link's speed-based value is link cost — path cost adds all hops to root.
incorrect.misconceptionTested: Link cost definition as path cost
incorrect.whatItDoes: Path cost is a numeric value associated with the speed of a link. implies many-inside-to-few-outside PAT/overload translation.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "explanation", Path cost is the calculation of all the ports in the path to the root bridge. satisfies what this question tests — Path cost is a numeric value associated with the speed of a link. does not.

answerReview.examTip: Root port pick: lowest path cost to root → tie-break port ID.

questions.question: Which statement is correct about the Common Spanning Tree (CST)?

incorrect.explanation: Per-VLAN root is PVST+/Rapid PVST+ behavior — CST shares one tree.

incorrect.whatItDoes: CST has an immediate convergence because it elects a single root bridge. points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for statement.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "statement", CST elects a single root bridge for the entire physical network. satisfies what this question tests — CST has an immediate convergence because it elects a single root bridge. does not.

incorrect.misconceptionTested: CST as best for large networks
incorrect.whatItDoes: CST is best implemented for really large networks because it scales efficiently. points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for statement.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "statement", CST elects a single root bridge for the entire physical network. satisfies what this question tests — CST is best implemented for really large networks because it scales efficiently. does not.

answerReview.examTip: CST = one STP for all VLANs | PVST+ = one STP per VLAN.

incorrect.whatItDoes: RSTP allows for multiple root bridges. points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for statement.
